title: Trump signals Iran peace progress as Hormuz attacks threaten talks
full_text:
Investing.com -- U.S. President Donald Trump said Washington was making progress in talks with Iran as Qatar urged both sides to reach a peace agreement, as incidents near the Strait of Hormuz raised escalation risks.
Speaking to reporters Friday, Trump said Iranian representatives wanted a deal and that negotiations were advancing. He also said U.S. forces had recently destroyed an Iranian air defense installation.
Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said mediation remained active and warned that negotiators should not wait for a perfect agreement. Doha rejected reports that talks had failed, saying its mediators remained in contact with Washington and Tehran.
The diplomatic push followed reports that two projectiles struck Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian authorities reported no casualties, while the country’s military claimed to have shot down an American drone over the island. U.S. Central Command described the situation around Qeshm as relatively calm.
Iran’s army separately warned that it would not allow damaged U.S. military bases in the region to be rebuilt. A senior Iranian lawmaker also threatened retaliation if Washington or Israel launched further attacks.
Shipping remained under pressure. The manager of the oil products tanker MT Velos said a crew member died after the vessel was struck by suspected projectiles in the Gulf on Thursday. Another tanker reported an explosion near its waterline while crossing Hormuz, with its crew safe.
Tehran has exempted vessels from China, India, Qatar and Iraq from some Hormuz restrictions, but the U.S. naval blockade continues to complicate maritime traffic.
Washington also imposed sanctions on eight Canada-based money services businesses accused of facilitating transactions involving sanctioned Iranian entities. The State Department warned Americans in the Middle East about possible Houthi attacks and threats to U.S. officials.
Regional fighting continued in Yemen, where government forces and Houthi rebels traded accusations over a deadly market attack. Saudi-led forces also reported intercepting drones near Riyadh and Mecca.
The disruption has added pressure to energy markets and regional shipping, raising the stakes for ongoing peace talks.

title: China extends gold buying streak to 24 months as prices slump below $4,000
full_text:
Investing.com -- China’s central bank increased its gold reserves for a 24th consecutive month in October, extending its buying streak to two years as bullion prices recorded their steepest October decline since 2008.
The People’s Bank of China added 830,000 troy ounces, equivalent to about 25.8 metric tons, according to official figures released Saturday. Purchases during the first 10 months of 2026 totaled approximately 129 tons.
The latest increase came as gold fell almost 7% in October, finishing the month below $4,000 an ounce after touching a one-year low. The decline marked the metal’s worst October performance since the global financial crisis.
China has accelerated its reserve accumulation in recent months, buying into a downturn that has tested investor confidence in the precious metal.
The central bank was the largest publicly disclosed official buyer in the third quarter, according to World Gold Council figures. Central banks worldwide reported net purchases of 321 tons between July and September, the strongest quarterly total since the final three months of 2024.
Official-sector demand has provided support for bullion at a time when other sources of buying have been subdued.
Gold has recovered some ground following this week’s U.S. midterm elections, although prices remain more than 20% below levels seen when the Iran war began in late February.
Higher energy costs linked to the conflict have increased inflationary pressures, encouraging tighter monetary policy. Higher interest rates tend to weigh on gold, which pays no interest.
The central bank’s continued purchases have also influenced retail demand in China, where households bought bullion near $4,000 an ounce during October in anticipation of longer-term price support.
Its purchases have continued amid significant volatility across global precious metals markets this year.
The latest reserve figures highlight the contrast between sustained official buying and the price weakness that has characterized gold trading in recent months.

title: Brent posts worst week since April 2020 amid post-midterms hopes for Iran detente
full_text:
Investing.com -- The global oil benchmark on Friday slumped nearly 17% for the week to post its worst weekly performance since late April 2020, as energy market participants assessed the implications of the Democratic midterm election victory on hopes for de-escalation between the U.S. and Iran.
Brent crude futures expiring in January dipped 0.6% to settle at $97.75 a barrel, while posting a 16.9% decline for the week. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures expiring in December shed 0.2% to settle at $90.36 a barrel, falling 13.2% for the week for their steepest weekly loss since mid-April. Traders have been gauging the implications of the decisive Democratic election win, which gave the party control over both chambers of Congress. Speculation has swirled around whether the Democrats will use their newfound influence to force Republican President Donald Trump to find a resolution to the Iran war.
"Although flips of the U.S. House and Senate had been broadly contemplated, heavy Democratic outperformance in the midterms forces a re-calibration of expectations with respect to the Iran War. In short, substantial majorities in each chamber of Congress increases costs to President Trump for continuing/escalating a broadly unpopular conflict," Walt Chancellor, energy strategist at Macquarie, said.
"While Trump would maintain considerable executive latitude to strike Iran, given the new complexion of Congress and its intrinsic budgetary authorities, for Trump, the ability to sustain these efforts to achieve strategic goals falls, and the opportunity costs associated with any such action rises. In the very near term, the midterms may change behavior/incentives for the administration, but they do not eliminate Trump’s executive prerogatives for military action (subject to limitations)," he said.
"To bind Trump from further engaging Iran, ultimately, a veto-proof majority from both chambers of Congress would be required; a seemingly high bar. As such, we do not believe the political calendar itself should create any great urgency to strike Iran during the ’lame-duck’ Congressional session; that option would ostensibly still be available in the New Year," Chancellor added.
A conclusion to the Middle East conflict, which began with a joint U.S.-Israeli assault on Iran in late February, could reopen critical shipping corridors in the Middle East. Recent shipping data have suggested that some oil supply flows out of the region are recovering partially due to naval security provided by the U.S. military, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz.
However, vessels remain alert to attacks in the vital waterway, through which about a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas flowed before the war. Iran moved to cut off the strait shortly after the conflict began.
Reports of fresh attacks on tankers in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz pushed up prices on Thursday. Data from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre, a maritime monitoring group, indicated that attacks on oil-bearing ships were still happening at close to record levels.
On Friday, de-escalation hopes were also boosted by media reports that Trump had discussed mediation efforts with Qatar’s Emir, Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.
Hovering in the background was an artificial intelligence-driven bloodbath in stock markets on Thursday triggered by fears that a Democrat-controlled Congress may support greater restrictions on the AI industry.

title: Peltola campaign sues Alaska to get records on rejected absentee ballots
full_text:
By Daniel Trotta
Nov 6 (Reuters) - The campaign of Democratic US Senate candidate Mary Peltola of Alaska sued state election officials on Friday seeking the immediate release of records identifying absentee ballots that were rejected in Tuesday’s voting.
Peltola and the Republican candidate, incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan remain locked in a close contest for the seat, with about 600 votes separating them as ballots from remote areas in the sprawling state were still being counted.
With such a narrow margin separating the candidates, the race could hinge on ballots that were mailed or that have to be flown in from remote communities. The state will accept ballots up to November 18.
Democrats captured control of the US Senate as part of their sweeping victory across the country in the midterm elections. The undecided Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi will determine whether the Democrats can expand on their 54-seat majority in the 100-member chamber.
Peltola’s campaign group, Alaskans for Mary, sued the Alaska Division of Elections, Lieutenant Governor Nancy Dahlstrom and Director of Elections Carol Beecher, seeking the release of records identifying absentee ballots rejected in Tuesday’s election and the reasons for those rejections.
The campaign says it requested the records on October 27 and again on Wednesday under Alaska’s Public Records Act but received no response, and was later denied immediate access.
The plaintiffs also sought a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction to compel the immediate release of the records, arguing that time is critical because ballot counting and certification are under way.
Friday’s filing argues that a lack of prompt access would leave Alaskans for Mary unable to monitor whether ballots are being properly counted and whether Peltola supporters had their ballots improperly rejected, as alleged in the lawsuit.
The state Department of Law, which represents the lieutenant governor and the Division of Elections, said in a statement that the Division of Elections has long treated those records as confidential and that Alaska law does not require their release.
"Because the information is preliminary, subject to change, and not yet available to affected voters, the Division does not distribute the records separately or allow observers to retain them," the statement said.
"Releasing preliminary information in the manner sought by the lawsuit would create additional burdens during ballot processing and could delay the timely counting of votes. The Division has protected this information for years and will ask the court to protect it too," the statement said.
Sullivan’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Russia launches ballistic missile attack on Kyiv ahead of Abu Dhabi peace talks
full_text:
Investing.com -- Russian forces launched a ballistic missile attack on Ukraine’s capital Kyiv, early Saturday, damaging residential buildings and injuring two people, just three days before U.S.-led peace talks involving Ukrainian and Russian negotiators.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported explosions in the capital’s suburbs, saying Russian forces were targeting infrastructure with ballistic missiles.
Debris from the strikes hit a five-storey apartment building in a western district of the city, damaging the structure. The facade of another residential building was also damaged.
The city’s military administration reported two injuries and damage to a building housing a kindergarten, highlighting the impact of the attack on civilian areas.
Authorities continued warning residents about the possibility of further strikes several hours after the initial explosions, indicating that the threat had not fully subsided.
The latest assault followed warnings from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy that Russian forces were preparing additional attacks against critical infrastructure.
In his nightly video address before the strikes, Zelenskiy said Moscow was planning operations targeting energy facilities, bridges and other infrastructure across Ukraine.
The warnings raised concerns about further disruption to civilian services and transport networks as the conflict continues into its fifth year.
The missile attack also comes ahead of renewed diplomatic efforts aimed at ending the war, with U.S.-led negotiations scheduled to begin in Abu Dhabi in three days.
Representatives from Ukraine and Russia are expected to participate in the discussions, marking another attempt to negotiate a settlement to the conflict that began more than four years ago.
The previous round of talks involving the two countries took place in February, leaving a lengthy gap before the upcoming meeting.
Officials had not provided a comprehensive assessment of infrastructure damage or indicated whether additional casualties had been reported following Saturday’s strikes.

title: Bitcoin rebounds to $76,000, but $1.3 billion ETF exodus tests recovery
full_text:
Investing.com -- Bitcoin was trading above $76,000 on Saturday, showing signs of stabilization after a bruising selloff, but another wave of withdrawals from U.S. exchange-traded funds highlighted the gap between its modest recovery and institutional demand.
The world’s leading cryptocurrency was trading up 0.59% at $76,103.2 as of 03:13 ET (08:13 GMT).
U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $411.9 million in net outflows on Friday, according to fund-flow data, extending a second consecutive session of withdrawals. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust accounted for $403 million in redemptions, offset partly by $42.8 million flowing into Fidelity’s fund.
The latest figures bring November’s net Bitcoin ETF withdrawals to roughly $1.28 billion through Friday, with Wednesday the only positive session of the month so far. The withdrawals suggest institutional investors have yet to provide sustained support following the cryptocurrency’s sharp decline.
Bitcoin had fallen about 5.2% over 24 hours during Friday’s earlier trading, after its rebound following the U.S. midterm elections faded. A broader technology-stock selloff, linked to worries over artificial intelligence spending and data-center development, weighed on risk appetite.
More than $1.27 billion in cryptocurrency derivatives positions were liquidated during that earlier 24-hour period, including over $1.1 billion in bullish bets. Forced selling amplified market volatility as traders reduced leveraged exposure.
The market is also assessing a tougher regulatory backdrop. U.S. Treasury officials moved to restrict cryptocurrency exchange MEXC’s access to American financial institutions, alleging that it processed at least $16 billion in suspicious transactions linked to sanctions evasion and other illicit activity between 2021 and 2026.
Separately, Greece approved a framework taxing cryptocurrency capital gains at 10% above an annual €500 threshold, with a 15% levy on staking, lending and decentralized-finance income beginning in January 2027.
Legal fallout from the FTX collapse continued as Binance and founder Changpeng Zhao sought records from investor Kevin O’Leary and author Michael Lewis in a $1.76 billion recovery dispute.
Longer-term security concerns also resurfaced after Bitcoin Core developer Cory Fields proposed a mechanism requiring potential quantum attackers to post Bitcoin collateral that legitimate owners could claim. The proposal remains conceptual and would require quantum-resistant wallets.
For traders, $80,000 remains a nearby recovery marker, with $73,000 cited as a possible downside level. The immediate test is whether Saturday’s bounce can hold without a reversal in ETF flows.

title: Fed’s Daly says further rate hikes likely needed to curb inflation
full_text:

"My expectation is, we're going to have to tighten policy further," Daly said during a CNBC interview, though she noted the exact timing and magnitude remains unclear. She pointed to ongoing volatility in multiple areas, saying "those volatilities are something that you have to take into account, collect more information, and be deliberate but more gradual in how you get there when you don't know exactly where you're going to need to head."

title: Trump administration drops California mail-in ballot lawsuit after midterms
full_text:
Investing.com -- The Trump administration withdrew a lawsuit Friday seeking to prevent California from counting mail-in ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters whom federal officials alleged were likely not U.S. citizens, ending the legal challenge after this week’s midterm elections.
The Justice Department filed a notice of voluntary dismissal after Democrats won California’s statewide races by comfortable margins and prevailed in most congressional contests.
The case centered on registered voters identified by federal officials as potentially ineligible to vote on citizenship grounds. The administration had sought to stop ballots associated with those voters from being counted.
On Monday, one day before the election, the U.S. Supreme Court rejected the administration’s request to temporarily block California from including the disputed ballots in its vote count.
In earlier court filings, Justice Department lawyers argued that immediate intervention was necessary as ballots could no longer be separated from other votes after election officials accepted them.
The department cited that same issue in Friday’s dismissal notice, saying the remedy it had requested was no longer possible after the ballots had been counted.
"The relief the United States sought is no longer available," the department wrote, explaining its decision to end the proceedings.
U.S. District Judge David Carter had previously questioned the administration’s request, raising concerns about the potential consequences for eligible voters and the administration of an election already underway.
Carter warned that the proposed intervention could confuse legitimate voters and prevent some from having their votes counted. He described the requested change to established election procedures as "monumental."
The case unfolded against the backdrop of California’s midterm voting, with federal officials pressing for action immediately before election day and the Supreme Court declining to intervene.
Friday’s filing came after the counting process had progressed beyond the point at which the Justice Department said its requested remedy could be implemented.

title: Musk cites Alphabet conflicts as Google executive leaves SpaceX board
full_text:
Investing.com -- SpaceX said Google executive Donald Harrison has resigned from its board of directors after more than a decade, with Elon Musk citing conflicts of interest involving Google’s parent company, Alphabet.
Harrison notified the company of his resignation on November 4, with the departure taking effect immediately, according to a regulatory disclosure released Friday.
The company said his resignation did not result from any disagreement concerning its operations, policies or practices.
Musk subsequently explained the departure in a post on X, saying Harrison faced too many conflicts of interest involving Alphabet.
The SpaceX chief executive also praised Harrison’s service, expressing appreciation for his contributions during his tenure on the board.
Harrison currently serves as Google’s president of Global Partnerships and Corporate Development, a senior position overseeing relationships and strategic business initiatives at the technology company.
His departure comes as Alphabet maintains a substantial investment in SpaceX, making it the company’s largest single institutional shareholder, according to LSEG data.
Google separately disclosed Friday that its SpaceX holdings had increased to approximately 555 million shares, compared with about 551.2 million shares previously.
The increase represents roughly 3.8 million additional shares, indicating that Alphabet’s investment position expanded around the time of Harrison’s departure.
The board change removes a senior Google representative from SpaceX’s leadership structure, although the disclosure did not indicate any change to the companies’ investment relationship.
Harrison’s resignation also comes as SpaceX operates across an expanding range of businesses, spanning rocket launches, satellite communications and artificial intelligence.
The combination of Alphabet’s significant ownership position and Harrison’s executive responsibilities at Google had created overlapping interests between the two companies, according to Musk’s explanation.
SpaceX did not identify specific transactions, commercial arrangements or board decisions that contributed to the conflicts cited by its chief executive.
The resignation took effect without any disclosed dispute over the company’s management or strategic direction.

title: Arini hedge fund losses deepen to 32% as credit selloff intensifies - Bloomberg
full_text:
Investing.com -- Arini Capital Management’s flagship hedge fund suffered losses of 32% this year after a sharp October decline, prompting the London-based credit specialist to reduce leverage and sell some holdings, Bloomberg reported exclusively, citing an investor letter.
The fund, managed by founder Hamza Lemssouguer, lost 19.7% in October as weakness in speculative-grade debt intensified. Its year-to-date decline had stood at approximately 26% as of October 23.
The losses reflect heavy exposure to CCC-rated corporate debt, among the riskiest segments of the credit market. The firm acknowledged underestimating the extent of the disruption, leaving its portfolio vulnerable to simultaneous declines across holdings.
Following the selloff, the fund reassessed its five largest investments, which account for roughly two-thirds of its net asset value.
It also reduced gross leverage to its lowest level since early 2022 and trimmed selected positions, with plans to increase portfolio diversification.
The adjustments come as the firm continues raising capital, attracting $389 million in investor inflows over the past week as part of a broader $1.5 billion fundraising effort.
The credit specialist attributed market weakness partly to technical pressures, including restrictions on purchases of CCC-rated securities by collateralized loan obligations and aggressive short selling.
Its portfolio includes debt issued by Altice International, Brightspeed and Aston Martin, companies facing financial pressures that have contributed to falling bond prices.
Some holdings have already been offered for sale, with prospective buyers including Pacific Investment Management Co. and Oaktree Capital Management. Initial transactions have focused primarily on more liquid, better-performing assets.
The firm maintained confidence in its largest investments after reviewing asset coverage, liquidity, recovery prospects, and creditor protections.
Arini has grown rapidly since launching with approximately $1 billion in 2022, reaching $21.7 billion in assets before the latest market turmoil.
A company representative had no immediate comment on the investor letter.

title: UK PM Burnham seeks closer EU ties as Brexit tensions threaten growth push

Investing.com -- British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is preparing to seek closer economic ties with the European Union at two November summits, testing whether the government can loosen Brexit-era restrictions without reviving political divisions at home.
The first test comes at next week’s European Political Community meeting in Dublin, followed by a formal UK-EU summit on November 20. British officials hope the meetings will give momentum to negotiations that have struggled over several issues.

Brussels also faces competing priorities, including discussions with Canada about a closer relationship with the bloc. European officials have expressed doubts that Britain’s more ambitious rhetoric will produce immediate changes in negotiations.
For Burnham, the challenge is securing meaningful trade concessions without promising a settlement that lacks durable support from Parliament, voters or European governments.

title: As COP31 comes to Turkey, satellites reveal a landfill methane problem
full_text:
By Ali Kucukgocmen
SEYMEN, Turkey, Nov 7 (Reuters) - In the countryside west of Istanbul, trucks line up to empty mixed household waste from the city of 16 million people onto a vast landscape of decomposing rubbish, where landfill gas is captured to generate electricity at a nearby plant.
But far above the seagulls circling the waste, satellites detect what the plant has failed to capture: methane escaping at a rate that ranks it among the world’s largest recorded landfill emitters.
Turkey hosts COP31 in Antalya from November 9 to 20 and has made methane reduction a priority for the climate summit.
Methane is the biggest cause of climate change after carbon dioxide (CO2) and is over 80 times more potent than CO2 in its first 20 years in the air. Sharp cuts could therefore slow warming relatively quickly.
Turkey’s waste sector illustrates both the potential and the difficulty of achieving rapid cuts.
The country is the world’s fifth-biggest emitter of methane from solid waste behind China, the United States, Russia and Brazil, according to data from non-profit emissions tracker Climate TRACE.
Satellite observations analysed by researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) identified 70 plumes from Turkey’s 10 highest-emitting waste sites, where average detected rates ranged from 841 kg to 7.4 metric tons an hour. Three were around Istanbul, while others were near Ankara, Izmir and Antalya, where COP31 is being held.
Gas capture is widespread at Turkey’s larger municipal landfills, indicating that collection systems alone do not prevent large releases.
’HUGE POTENTIAL’
Tia Scarpelli, waste sector lead for emissions-monitoring non-profit Carbon Mapper, said cutting landfill methane requires diverting organic material before it reaches dumps, while improving rates of capture.
Because Turkey’s largest detected emissions were concentrated at a few sites, addressing those landfills could deliver disproportionate gains, Scarpelli said.
“There is this huge mitigation potential by just addressing the largest landfills to reduce their national emissions,” she said, suggesting better-designed collection systems and repairs to cracked covers or faulty gas wells.
The UCLA analysis used public Carbon Mapper data from the Tanager-1 satellite between January 2025 and end-May 2026.
It showed an average detected rate of about 7.4 tons an hour from the landfill west of Istanbul near Seymen — just below the highest-emitting landfill on a global list from 2025.
“What stands out is how big its emissions are and how persistently large they are,” said Scarpelli.
In response to a request for comment, Turkey’s Environment Ministry said the data were not from continuous measurements and could not be used to measure annual emissions at the Seymen landfill.
It said Turkey’s Zero Waste Initiative, a government scheme to promote recycling, aims to reduce waste going to landfills, thereby lowering methane emissions, adding that the national "recovery rate" for waste had risen to 37.53% in 2025 from 13% in 2017.
At the Seymen landfill, municipal operator ISTAC collects gas produced as buried organic material decomposes, while an energy company burns the gas to generate electricity at a plant opened in 2020.
The facility produces about 22,000 megawatt-hours of electricity a month, according to a 2025 report by energy news website Enerji Gunlugu.
ISTAC benefits economically from efficient methane capture to produce electricity, the Environment Ministry said.
ISTAC official Aysen Erdincler disputed whether the satellite observations were representative of the landfill’s emissions, saying they typically ranged between 4 and 6 tons per hour, while a satellite reading of 12 tons per hour on one day had raised the average. ISTAC head Fatih Ugur said about 30 hectares of the landfill had been left uncovered on the day of that measurement while work was carried out on methane-collection pipes, and that low atmospheric pressure had also contributed to a higher concentration of methane.
The Seymen site takes some 8,500 tons of household waste daily, from Istanbul’s average total of 20,000 tons, according to ISTAC. It is unclear to researchers how much of the landfill’s methane the system captures, but Erdincler said methane leaks at the site were usually around 25%.
TURKEY ABSENT FROM METHANE PLEDGE
Methane emissions from waste in Turkey rose nearly 25% in the decade to 2024, compared to a global rise of 6.5% over the same period, according to World Bank data based on the European Commission’s EDGAR emissions database. Turkey’s waste emissions have remained around 21 million tons of CO2 equivalent annually since 2020.
In 2021, the Global Methane Pledge (GMP) was launched at COP26, seeking a collective 30% cut in methane emissions from 2020 levels by 2030, with more than 30 countries later backing national targets. Turkey is not listed among the pledge’s participants.
Selim Yildirim, chief climate policy researcher at Ankara-based D84, a non-profit policy and media platform, said Turkey had more developed waste disposal than poorer countries but less effective management, recycling and value recovery than much of Europe.
Turkey could still join the GMP during COP31, he said, but that would not guarantee results.
"The issue is whether you can effectively turn it into action and implement it,” he said, adding that regulation was needed to push operators to capture and reuse methane.
In Seymen, about 5 km (3 miles) from the landfill, residents have another concern — the smell. Methane itself is odourless, but the decomposing organic waste can also release pungent compounds.
In summer, it enters through windows left open against the heat, said Soner Duz, a 46-year-old barber.
“Around four or five in the morning, the smell suddenly comes," he said. "It wakes you up.”

title: Environmental groups embrace AI, even as they warn of data center impacts
full_text:
By Valerie Volcovici
WASHINGTON, Nov 7 (Reuters) - Environmental groups worldwide are using artificial intelligence to analyze climate data, track forest fires and count endangered wildlife – embracing a technology they also warn is driving a surge in electricity demand, water use and greenhouse-gas emissions.
The contradiction is forcing these organizations to justify their AI use in carrying out missions to combat climate change or protect natural resources.
"We recognize that AI can come with environmental costs, and we need to be thoughtful about how we use it," said Ali Swanson, AI lead at the US nonprofit Conservation International. "But at a time when the climate and biodiversity crises are becoming more urgent, AI can help us move faster and make better use of the information we’re collecting."
The group recently started using AI to assess hotspots detected by satellites and send real-time alerts to community forest patrols about potential wildfires in remote and environmentally sensitive parts of Cambodia.
Reuters interviewed 15 major environmental, conservation and development organizations about their AI use. All said they used the technology in some form and expressed concern about the environmental impact of the data centers powering it. The centers, filled with servers, can require vast amounts of electricity, along with water for cooling.
It’s a global dilemma for individuals, governments and industries balancing AI’s benefits with its enormous risks. The tradeoffs likely will grab attention at the UN’s COP31 climate conference this month, when host Turkey will call on governments, businesses and other institutions to sign a pledge outlining principles to ensure AI is developed and deployed sustainably.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres wants major AI companies to publicly disclose their systems’ environmental impacts.
Researchers at the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health estimate the global data-center footprint could more than double by 2030, reaching a size about twice that of Jakarta, the Indonesian megalopolis.
The International Energy Agency, meanwhile, estimates global data centers will consume about 945 terawatt-hours of electricity annually by 2030, producing the equivalent of more than 300 million metric tons of carbon dioxide. That’s double current consumption and about equal to Japan’s annual electricity use.
The agency also projects that global data center water consumption will increase from about 560 billion liters (147.9 billion gallons) in 2023 to about 1.2 trillion liters (317 billion gallons) annually by 2030.
Technology giants including Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet’s Google have reported rising emissions linked in part to data center expansion, raising questions about their ability to meet their own long-term climate goals.
Amazon told Reuters its artificial-intelligence products were among the most sustainable due to the company’s purchases of low-carbon energy and its efforts to use power and water efficiently.
Microsoft and Google didn’t respond to requests for comment.
BREAKTHROUGHS ONCE THOUGHT IMPOSSIBLE
Many of the organizations that spoke to Reuters believe AI’s benefits currently outweigh its costs because the technology is enabling work that was previously difficult, expensive or impossible.
Kenya’s Save the Elephants, a partner of the Wildlife Conservation Network, said it is using machine learning to improve population surveys and study elephant communication.
Frank Pope, the group’s chief executive, said an aerial survey of Kenya’s largest protected area last year generated roughly 200,000 images that took nine people nine months to review manually. AI models trained on Nvidia’s GeForce graphics platforms can now complete similar analyses in hours.
"The results have been eye-opening," Pope said. "We found that human surveys were missing about a third of the elephants, roughly half of zebras and giraffes, and three-quarters of oryx populations."
More accurate wildlife data can help secure financing for conservation, he said.
"Ultimately, these tools make nature measurable and therefore investable," he said. "That’s a critical transformation, if we’re going to conserve biodiversity at scale."
At the institute founded by the late conservation icon Jane Goodall, researchers are using AI to digitize decades of field notes about chimpanzee behavior in Tanzania’s Gombe National Park.
The project was once expected to take 13-15 years because the records were written by hand using the local Kiha language and scientific shorthand.
Thanks to a tool developed with Amazon Web Services, the notes can now be scanned, translated and structured in minutes, slashing the time needed to about two years, said Lilian Pintea, the Jane Goodall Institute’s vice president of conservation science.
During her lifetime, Pintea said, Goodall supported the use of AI to advance conservation science, provided people remained firmly in control of how it was used.
"AI technology should be seen as tools which are human-centered," Pintea said.
LIMITING THE ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT
Some organizations are experimenting with ways to limit the environmental impact of their AI use.
The World Resources Institute (WRI), a research group that uses AI to accelerate its climate and environmental analyses, said it limits resource-intensive applications such as generating videos and images, while caching AI query results so identical searches don’t need to be reprocessed.
The US-based Nature Conservancy has adopted a similar approach. It uses AI to analyze video captured on commercial fishing vessels for information on how many fish of different species they catch. But instead of uploading huge numbers of videos to centralized data centers, it has installed AI-powered digital cameras to process information aboard the vessels, reducing energy use and data-transfer requirements, said Vienna Saccomanno, a senior scientist at the organization.
"It takes a lot of engineering to make computation on the edge possible," she said. "This was worth it to reduce both our carbon footprint and deliver these sustainability insights."
Greenpeace International said it, too, uses some AI tools, mainly because software platforms it relies upon include AI features.
It’s imposing internal guidelines emphasizing transparency, human oversight and "intentional" AI use, the group said. But it would prefer to sidestep the technology due to its environmental impacts and is pushing back hard on the data center buildout.
"While other organizations are asking how to use AI responsibly, Greenpeace is asking whether it’s necessary to build all these massive data centers in the first place," said Katrin Xueying Wu, a climate and energy campaigner with the organization.
Other groups now see AI as vital to effective environmental activism.
"It’s our job to save the planet. If we can do that more effectively and efficiently with the limited resources we’ve got by using AI, then we have to seriously engage in that possibility," said Stuart Butchart, chief scientist at UK-based BirdLife International.
"If we don’t do it, then we’re sort of being derelict in our duty."
(Additonal reporting by Simon Jessop in London and Kate Abnett in Brussels; Editing by Richard Valdmanis and Alexandra Zavis)

title: French presidential hopeful Melenchon pledges minimum wage rise, retirement at 60
full_text:
By Mathieu Rosemain
PARIS, Nov 7 (Reuters) - Jean-Luc Melenchon, the hard-left French presidential hopeful, will pledge to raise the minimum wage and restore the country’s retirement age to 60 when he launches his 2027 election programme on Saturday.
Melenchon, 75, is viewed as the strongest contender on the left and recent opinion polls have shown him reaching the presidential runoff next April against Marine Le Pen on the far-right, but also indicate he would lose in the second round.
His manifesto, titled "L’Avenir en commun" ("A Shared Future"), is the fifth edition of the platform of his party, France Unbowed (LFI), and largely reaffirms policies that have formed the backbone of Melenchon’s previous presidential bids.
Among its flagship pledges is the repeal of President Emmanuel Macron’s pension reform, which gradually raised France’s minimum retirement age from 62 to 64 in an effort to shore up public finances.
LFI says it would restore retirement at 60 for people who have contributed to the system for 40 years.
The programme also calls for increasing the net monthly minimum wage to €1,700 from around €1,480 and includes plans to abolish the flat tax on capital income, raise taxes on the wealthiest households and cap prices for essential foods.
LFI also reiterates its support for a gradual phase-out of nuclear power in favour of a fully renewable electricity system, including scrapping the planned EPR2 reactor programme and not extending the lifespan of nuclear plants beyond 60 years.
On foreign policy, Melenchon’s programme reiterates his long-standing criticism of NATO and calls for France’s gradual withdrawal from the alliance, starting with an exit from its integrated military command.
It also criticises German influence on European Union economic policy, describing Berlin as Europe’s chief defender of "ordoliberalism", an economic philosophy centred on strict budget rules, price stability and independent monetary policy.
The programme calls for greater protection of domestic industry, including measures to encourage the relocation of production to France, and advocates a more interventionist role for the state in the economy.

title: Exclusive-Rubio seeks to impose order at State as Republicans look ahead to 2028
full_text:
By Gram Slattery, Humeyra Pamuk and Jonathan Landay
WASHINGTON, Nov 7 (Reuters) - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has moved to tighten control over the State Department, telling senior officials in a recent meeting that staff must stay in their lanes and avoid efforts that present conflicts of interest, four people familiar with the matter said.
Rubio’s message, delivered last week before the Republican Party’s electoral losses this Tuesday, comes as the party’s leading figures attempt to put distance between themselves and an increasingly unpopular Trump administration.
The meeting followed the high-profile resignation of US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle in mid-October after news reports raised concerns that she sold access to Trump administration officials in exchange for money, gifts and favors.
Guilfoyle has called the reports false and in a post on social media said she would defend her reputation.
Rubio told the meeting, which included many of the roughly two dozen assistant secretaries of state, that unethical behavior would result in a firing, regardless of how well-connected an official might be, said one of the people.
He added that too many officials were making decisions or pushing policy agendas without coordinating and that significant decisions required his signoff or that of Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, according to the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Details of the meeting have not previously been reported.
The State Department declined to comment on the meeting.
Soon after the meeting, three of the people said, the State Department’s policy chief, Jeremy Lewin, was forced out of his job in part due to concerns that he was working on matters outside his area without proper coordination. The exact details of those concerns remain unclear.
None of the people who spoke to Reuters suggested Lewin’s departure was linked to any incidents of ethical misconduct. By Yasmeen Abutaleb, Richard Cowan, Nolan D. McCaskill and Tim Reid
WASHINGTON, Nov 7 (Reuters) - Four years after helping Democrats win both US Senate seats in Georgia, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer went looking for a candidate who could expand the party’s map.
He found one in an unlikely place: Mississippi.
Public prosecutor Scott Colom had seen his path to becoming the state’s first Black federal judge in more than a century blocked in 2023 by US Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Mississippi Republican. Now Schumer wanted him to take on Hyde-Smith for her Senate seat. So intent was Schumer to recruit Colom that he invited him and his father to brunch in November 2024.
"I said you’ve got to run," he told the news channel MS Now.
Two years later, Colom will become the first Black senator from Mississippi since post-Civil War Reconstruction if his 2,000-vote lead holds.
"Mississippi has always been overlooked or at the bottom of things nationally," Colom told reporters on Friday, as election officials counted provisional ballots. "But I think that this race is going to make a difference in our nation."
Colom’s improbable run was part of an ambitious Democratic push to compete in races long considered unwinnable, betting that rising costs, voter unease with President Donald Trump and strong local candidates could put Republican territory in play.
The gamble paid off in Tuesday’s midterm elections when Democrats seized control of both houses of Congress from Republicans, the result of a string of victories in Republican strongholds including Kansas and Texas.
The question now is whether Democrats benefited from an extraordinary political moment or found a playbook they can use again.
In any event, Democratic leaders said they planned to go on pursuing victories in states they had previously written off as guaranteed Republican wins.
"We need to make sure that we’re competing everywhere. We should not be ceding ground (to Republicans)," said Anderson Clayton, chair of the North Carolina Democratic Party. "I get that everybody is really excited – and I am, too – but I’m also looking at where did we have opportunities that we missed."
ORGANIZING TO WIN EVERYWHERE
The strategy rested on a belief that the usual midterm backlash against the party in the White House would be amplified by voter frustration with Trump and the rising cost of living, creating an opportunity to expand the electoral map.
Democrats invested more broadly in party organizations across the country rather than concentrating resources in a handful of traditional battlegrounds.
“Do you invest in the battleground states or do you invest in all 57 state parties so you can organize year-round and organize to win anywhere?” Jane Kleeb, vice chair of the Democratic National Committee, said. “Obviously (DNC Chair Ken) Martin chose that we’re going to win everywhere and he got a lot of hell for it. People were calling for his head.”
Elsewhere, some races were considered such long shots that national party leaders had no contact with the Democratic candidates, only to find themselves searching for their phone numbers after they won.
By early 2026, Democratic polling showed voters shifting toward the party on the economy, traditionally a Republican strength.
Strategists said Trump’s tariffs on foreign goods and the rise in fuel prices after he launched the war against Iran in February accelerated those trends and convinced many Democrats they could compete deeper into Republican turf.
REPUBLICANS GROW FRUSTRATED
As the year wore on, Republicans grew increasingly frustrated at Trump’s handling of the war in Iran and his decision not to focus on voters’ overwhelming top concern: the cost of living.
Democrats saw an opening, particularly as Trump’s approval ratings fell and fuel prices climbed. After Democrats’ sweep this week, numerous administration officials and Republican lawmakers were furious that Trump remained focused on White House construction projects and tried to distance himself from Tuesday’s results.
“How hard is it to just acknowledge what voters are feeling?” one senior administration official said.
Democratic leaders were adamant they not repeat what they saw as the mistake of Trump’s first term by running only against him. Instead, they urged candidates to put forward their own proposals and convince voters they could deliver relief.
On election night, Democrats watched Republican-drawn districts across the country fall their way. In North Carolina, where Republicans redrew the map to try to control 11 of 14 House seats, their losses extended into districts Trump won by double digits.
Democrats are poised to capture 10 of the 14 seats. The national party had not even been in touch with several of its House candidates because their races were considered long shots and Republicans had far more cash, according to three Democratic strategists and campaign officials.
KEEP THE FOCUS ON AFFORDABILITY
After Trump ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in a US military operation in January, Democratic leaders gathered House members to deliver a simple message, according to party officials: Stay focused on economic issues at home.
Republicans had just allowed government-funded healthcare subsidies to expire, leaving voters facing higher costs.
One of the Democrats’ unlikeliest wins was in Kansas, where Democrats had not notched a US Senate win since 1932. Adam Hamilton, who won on Tuesday, entered the race only in April, and the national party did not focus on his campaign until the closing weeks, campaign adviser Guy Cecil told Reuters.
"We need to expand our idea of what’s possible," Cecil said of the Democratic Party. "We obviously included issues around affordability. But Adam talked a lot about restoring decency to the process and bringing people together."

title: After midterm rout, Vance tries to build his own 2028 brand
full_text:
By Jacob Bogage
WASHINGTON, Nov 7 (Reuters) - Late in his blitz to salvage Republicans’ midterm fortunes, Vice President JD Vance shifted strategy. He talked less about President Donald Trump and more about the issues that define his own political identity.
Vance argued the case for Republicans, who lost control of Congress in Tuesday’s vote, almost exclusively through the lens of his policy portfolio, according to a Reuters review of half a dozen speeches since the Republican convention in September.
He bypassed Trump’s signature policies including the Iran war and deportations as polls showed the president’s sagging popularity dragging down Republican office-seekers.
The change was deliberate, according to two people familiar with the strategy. Vance and his advisers saw the issues he championed — economic nationalism, foreign policy restraint, and public safety — as politically potent subjects he could address with authority. While Trump embraced them as part of his MAGA movement, Vance had emerged as their lead crusader, the people said.
The shift offered an early glimpse of how the 42-year-old vice president could chart his own course as Republicans begin looking beyond Trump.
Vance hasn’t said whether he will run for president in 2028, and Trump hasn’t endorsed him or anyone else. But Vance is viewed as a leading potential contender who some Republican officials say will need to inherit much of Trump’s coalition while separating himself from his boss’s baggage.
Vance took a more public step on Wednesday toward reinforcing his own political brand with an unusually blunt election postmortem. In a social media post, he blamed the Iran war for Republicans’ midterm defeat and laid out a platform for a Republican rebound.
He called for a swift end to the conflict and urged Republicans to focus on affordability, reevaluate foreign relations and overhaul the US relationship with Israel.
Trump has called Americans’ affordability concerns a Democratic “hoax.” He launched a war against Iran following sustained lobbying from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Trump went on to endorse Netanyahu in the Israeli election.
VANCE MAKES UNEASE AT THE WAR PUBLIC
The post for the first time put Vance openly on the side of ending the war.
Three people familiar with the White House and Vance’s communications told Reuters that the vice president was not breaking with Trump and said White House chief of staff Susie Wiles knew in advance about Vance’s post.
On Friday, Trump reshuffled senior White House leadership, replacing Wiles with Stephen Miller in a move that suggests the White House plans to double down on some of Trump’s more hardline policies.
Trump has acknowledged the Iran war played a role in the Republican rout because of the resulting high gas prices but has continued to defend it. "I would have done nothing different," he told reporters on Wednesday.
Reuters could not determine whether Trump was aware of the post in advance.
Donald Trump Jr., the president’s eldest son, endorsed Vance’s remarks on social media, along with some conservative allies.
The dialogue further elevated Vance as a potential post-Trump conservative standard-bearer, said Michael Ricci, a Republican strategist and former adviser to House Speakers John Boehner and Paul Ryan.
USING THE MEGAPHONE OF THE VICE PRESIDENCY
He said Vance’s message forced conservatives to debate the merits of the war, and more broadly, what core tenets Republican presidential candidates should embrace in 2028.
"It’s simplistic to say this about him looking for ways to differentiate himself from Trump," Ricci said. "This is about him using his megaphone of the vice presidency to set the terms of debate."
Representatives for Vance declined to comment. White House representatives referred Reuters to Trump’s comments on Wednesday, when he told reporters he understood Vance’s perspective on the election results.
Democrats are poised to tie Vance – or any Republican nominee – to Trump in 2028, especially if Trump plays a large role in vetting conservative hopefuls.
"There’s a real challenge of how you position yourself to be viable in a general election while winning a primary that still requires you to bow down and kiss the ring,” said Igor Volsky, a Democratic strategist.
Vance’s brand did not emerge from the midterms unscathed. Republicans lost in states where he campaigned. Some of the strategies he endorsed – including an ad by Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy that cast doubt on the sexual abuse suffered by the victorious Democratic candidate, Amy Acton – may have swung races away from Republicans.
Other possible 2028 presidential contenders have offered their diagnoses of the midterm defeat. US Senator Ted Cruz of Texas said Republicans hadn’t done enough on affordability. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said losing candidates had focused too heavily on transgender issues and neglected voter concerns about data centers and artificial intelligence. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has stayed silent.
Vance’s effort to shape the debate was visible during the closing days of the campaign.
In stump speeches, he told voters to support Republicans because they would investigate fraud in federal health care and antipoverty programs, tying that to the White House’s immigration agenda and cost of living. He almost entirely ignored the Iran war and gas prices, and seldom mentioned Trump by name.
“I want my kids to raise a family in a country that is vibrant and thriving and free and prosperous. I want the simple things,” Vance told one of his final rallies in North Carolina. “And because I want that for me, I want it for you too.”

ASUNCION, Nov 7 (Reuters) - Paraguay’s Vice President Pedro Alliana became president after the country’s Senate impeached and removed Santiago Peña amid a banking crisis that triggered major political backlash.

Alliana, 52, will serve out the remainder of Peña’s term through August 2028.
A longtime Colorado Party leader who had hoped to cap decades of political activism with a presidential run in 2028, Alliana achieved his goal two years early.

Peña had been a business partner in the group that owned the lender until March 2025.
For seven years, Alliana served as president of the Colorado Party, which has governed Paraguay for most of the last eight decades, and climbed the political ranks alongside former President Horacio Cartes.
"An Alliana presidency means policy continuity, dependence on Cartes and a weak mandate," said Mariano Machado, Americas principal analyst at Verisk Maplecroft. title: US anti-trans ballot wins pose challenge for Democrats ahead of 2028
full_text:
By Leah Douglas
WASHINGTON, Nov 7 (Reuters) - Voters in four US states approved ballot measures to restrict transgender rights in Tuesday’s midterm elections, sending a warning to Democrats on an issue that has divided the party and is likely to remain a political challenge heading into the 2028 presidential race.
The measures succeeded even as Democrats swept to victory nationwide and retook control of Congress, suggesting voters who backed Democratic candidates were still receptive to some Republican arguments on transgender issues.
Republicans hammered Democrats in midterm campaigns with attack ads painting their opponents as overly liberal on issues like the inclusion of transgender girls in sports, and gender-affirming care for minors.
Democratic candidates were divided in their responses. Some adopted more conservative postures on the issues, some maintained pro-transgender positions and others sidestepped a topic that Republicans wielded effectively against Democrats in the 2024 election.
Voters in Washington, Colorado, Arizona and Nebraska approved ballot measures prohibiting transgender children from playing on sports teams matching their gender identity or banning gender-affirming surgeries for minors.
The success of the ballot measures was "disheartening," said Rachel Tomlinson Dick, executive director of LGBTQ advocacy group Out Nebraska, adding that they expect to see similar measures on future ballots.
Democrats were caught flat-footed against Republican attacks on transgender issues in the 2024 presidential campaign. The party’s struggle to deliver a coherent response was widely seen as a contributor to former Vice President Kamala Harris’ loss to Trump.
This midterm cycle, candidates responded by emphasizing the need for fairness and rules in sports, which diluted Republican attacks, said Lanae Erickson, senior vice president at Third Way, a think tank that promotes political centrism.
Three of the states that passed anti-trans ballot measures - Washington, Colorado and Arizona - also elected Democrats to a majority of their state and federal seats.
But the success of the measures shows the party still needs to hone a message that appeals to a broad public, Erickson said.
"This week has shown us that Democrats have found effective ways to counter the anti-trans attacks when it comes to candidates, but that doesn’t necessarily mean that they’ve done the work to persuade voters on the issues," said Erickson, who consulted with Democratic midterm candidates on their approach to transgender issues.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll in April found that 67% of survey respondents supported banning transgender people from competing in female school sports. Ninety-two percent of Republicans said they supported such bans, compared with just 44% of Democrats.
Critics warn, however, that moving toward Republicans on trans issues is unlikely to win Democrats new support, and risks alienating LGBTQ voters and the party’s ascendant progressive wing.
The Democratic National Committee did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
MEASURES BAN TRANS ATHLETES, SURGERIES
Some transgender advocates said Tuesday’s electoral outcome was still promising even with the passage of the ballot measures.
The surge of support for Democrats, including some like Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, who supported transgender rights, showed the limits of the Republican Party’s anti-trans campaign strategy, said Lexi Koren, a communications consultant for No Hate in WA State, a coalition group that opposed Washington’s two ballot measures on trans issues.
"It was a resounding failure," she said.
Several states including Alabama and Michigan also elected transgender state lawmakers for the first time on Tuesday.
Twenty-seven states had laws in place before Tuesday restricting trans participation in youth sports, according to the nonprofit think tank Movement Advancement Project. That includes Nebraska, whose ballot initiative enshrined the ban in the state constitution.
Two other ballot measures on transgender issues were defeated on Tuesday.
One, in Washington state, would have expanded parental access to school records, potentially enabling parents to learn about a student’s gender identity against the child’s will. Another, in Missouri, would have prohibited gender-affirming care for minors, and also would have repealed the right to abortion.
Even where ballot measures lost, transgender people are still harmed by anti-trans rhetoric proliferating in politics, said Rodrigo Heng-Lehtinen, senior vice president at the Trevor Project, an advocacy group for LGBTQ youth.
"That kind of cultural hostility is not going to go away overnight," he said.

title: ECB’s Lagarde says inflation to stay high, sees little reason to alter rate course
full_text:
Investing.com - Euro zone inflation will remain elevated over the coming quarters, European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said, signaling that it would take "significant changes" to deter policymakers from raising interest rates again in December.
In an interview published Saturday by Japanese newspaper Yomiuri Shimbun, Lagarde noted that while price pressures are set to persist, secondary inflation pass-through has so far developed within the central bank’s expectations.
"We know that inflation numbers will remain high in the quarters to come," Lagarde told the newspaper. "The higher they are, and the longer they remain high, the greater the risk to our medium-term target."
The remarks follow the ECB’s decision in late October to hold its benchmark deposit rate steady at 2.50%. However, with headline inflation across the 21-member currency bloc running at double the central bank’s 2% objective - fueled by the surge in global crude and European natural gas prices since the eruption of the Middle East conflict - Governing Council hawks have increasingly pushed for renewed tightening.
Gauging wages and financial conditions
While core inflation held unchanged in October at 2.5%, Lagarde indicated that policymakers will scrutinize granular components before deciding whether to deliver a 25-basis-point hike next month, which would mark the third rate increase of the current cycle.
Crucially, the ECB chief noted that wage metrics have not yet triggered an alarming upward spiral.
"For the moment, we’re not seeing second-round effects beyond what we have incorporated in our projections," Lagarde said. "We’re watching carefully the forward-looking indicators - multi-year wage agreements, companies’ wage expectations - and we don’t see evidence of a shift yet."
ECB Policy Outlook & Macroeconomic Setting
Growth dilemma and succession race
A central challenge confronting policymakers is whether further tightening risks derailing economic momentum across the euro area. An additional quarter-point hike in December would push borrowing costs to the upper bound of the neutral policy range, beyond which interest rates actively restrict growth.
Furthermore, the recent worldwide surge in sovereign bond yields - spurred by heavy corporate debt issuance and heightened sovereign risk premiums, as seen in French 10-year OAT yields - is already exerting restrictive pressure on credit channels.
Despite those cross-currents, Lagarde reiterated that the bias remains toward tighter policy.
"I cannot tell you today that we will for sure do this in December," she said. "What I know is that, on the basis of the information we have today, it would take significant changes for the direction of travel to be different from what I expect."
The looming rate decision coincides with a leadership transition at the helm of European monetary policy. Lagarde, 70, announced last month that she will step down in February 2027, nine months before the formal end of her term. The Eurogroup confirmed on Friday that Dutch central bank chief Klaas Knot and former Bank of Spain Governor Pablo Hernández de Cos have emerged as the leading candidates to succeed her.

title: Novartis shelves potential blockbuster pelacarsen as landmark study fails
full_text:
Investing.com - Novartis AG is largely abandoning the development of its experimental cardiovascular drug pelacarsen, once projected to be a multi-billion-dollar blockbuster, after full study data showed it failed to reduce heart attacks, strokes, or cardiovascular deaths despite drastically lowering a key form of cholesterol.
The Swiss drugmaker said on Saturday it will halt development of the injectable therapy for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, the overarching condition behind heart attacks and strokes. Novartis will keep only a single mid-stage clinical study active to evaluate whether the drug can slow calcific aortic valve stenosis, a heart valve calcification disorder.
The decision follows the long-awaited presentation of detailed findings from the landmark Lp(a) HORIZON trial on Saturday at the American Heart Association scientific sessions in Chicago, alongside simultaneous publication in the New England Journal of Medicine.
The trial results deal a major blow to an experimental class of therapies targeting lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a)—a genetically inherited, cholesterol-carrying particle that promotes arterial clotting and plaque accumulation. While pelacarsen successfully drove down circulating Lp(a) levels by an average of 78%, the reduction generated zero clinical benefit in curbing cardiovascular events across every subgroup tested.
’Stone cold neutral’
"The trial is completely neutral," said Dr. Steven Nissen, chief academic officer at the Cleveland Clinic’s Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute and senior author of the study to Bloomberg.
"It is not harmful. It is not helpful. It is just stone cold neutral."
Novartis’s seven-year trial, which enrolled 8,322 patients with pre-existing cardiovascular disease and elevated Lp(a), was the first Phase 3 cardiovascular outcomes study in the industry to reach completion for this biological pathway.
Cardiologists and Wall Street analysts had broadly anticipated that clearing the particle would establish an entirely new pillar of preventive heart medicine, filling a major treatment void for the estimated 20% of the global population with high genetic levels unresponsive to statins or lifestyle modifications.
The medical community was left blindsided in September when Novartis issued a brief statement disclosing that the trial had missed its primary endpoints, withholding granular data until Saturday’s medical congress.

title: Why gold is losing its shine: Goldman breaks down the recent sell-off
full_text:
Investing.com - Speculative gold selling accelerated in late October, driving prices lower and decoupling the precious metal from falling real interest rates as non-traditional investors liquidated massive positions.
Managed Money, "Other," and Non-Reportable traders offloaded $8 billion in gold positions between Oct. 20 and Oct. 27, according to Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Commitment of Traders data. The sell-off marks a fifth consecutive week of bearish flows, bringing cumulative speculative outflows to $19.5 billion since Sept. 22.
The weekly outflow was driven by $5.2 billion in long liquidations and $2.8 billion in newly established short positions.
Categorically, the selling was overwhelmingly dominated by "Other" and Non-Reportable traders, which accounted for approximately 95% of the total outflows. Gross long selling by the "Other" category alone totaled $4 billion.
Yields ignored as dollar and oil bite
The aggressive liquidation helps explain gold’s lackluster price action during the period. The precious metal slipped 1.6% during the observation window, seemingly ignoring an 11-basis-point drop in U.S. 10-year real yields - a macroeconomic shift that typically provides a tailwind for non-yielding bullion.
Instead, gold faced headwinds from a 0.6% strengthening in the U.S. dollar and a 4.1% rally in Brent crude oil. Analysts noted that fears surrounding sovereign liquidity management and the resilience of the greenback likely sparked the unwinding of "Other" positions. Rolling six-month correlations for "Other" gross longs versus both the dollar index (DXY) and the front-month Brent contract have been moderately negative.
Despite the heavy selling, the market setup remains challenging for gold bulls. While Managed Money net positioning has stayed relatively low, "Other" gross long positions on Oct. 27 remained above their two-year median in both notional terms and as a percentage of open interest, leaving the door open for further long liquidations.
Gold’s weakness deepened into the end of the month, with the metal shedding an additional 4.3% between Oct. 27 and Oct. 30. Another 3.7% surge in Brent crude prices during those final days appeared to completely overshadow slight retracements in both the dollar and real yields.
The extended slide prompted a reaction in the derivatives market, where changes in the options surface indicated active downside hedging and outright bearish bets. Gold’s three-month implied volatility richened, while the normalized 25-delta put-call skew spiked to the 85th percentile of its one-year range.

title: Equity positioning suffered one of its sharpest weekly drops on record: DB
full_text:
Investing.com - Global equity positioning has plummeted to a massive underweight, registering one of the sharpest weekly declines on record as forced unwinding hammered the technology sector, according to a new research report from Deutsche Bank.
The firm’s consolidated measure of equity positioning plunged to the 20th percentile. Discretionary investors drove the retreat, with their positioning tumbling to the bottom 3% of its historical band, while systematic strategies rapidly slashed their exposure back to neutral.
The rapid exit signals extreme investor pessimism, with large-cap positioning now aligning with expectations of zero corporate earnings growth. Deutsche Bank strategists noted this sharply contradicts current market fundamentals, given the median S&P 500 company just posted nearly 15% earnings growth in the third quarter.
Technology stocks served as the epicenter of the rout, with sector positioning breaking below the broader market to hit lows unseen since "Liberation Day". Current positioning implies that tech earnings growth is turning negative, despite the sector posting a massive 53% aggregate growth rate in the third quarter.
While market chatter blamed the tech sell-off on the recent "blue sweep" in the U.S. mid-terms - sparking fears over bipartisan opposition to data center expansions - Deutsche Bank attributed the plunge primarily to a "forced positioning unwind".
Despite the grim sentiment, the bank remains aggressively bullish on the sector. Strategists reiterated an "overweight" rating on tech, arguing the recent collapse has created a highly favorable risk-reward setup and describing the market as a coiled spring.
Surprisingly, the massive positioning unwind coincided with aggressive capital allocations. Global equity funds absorbed $89.2 billion over the week, hitting a 20-week high.
This surge was dominated by emerging markets, which registered a record $45.1 billion influx. Chinese equities absorbed the bulk of the emerging market flows with $34.5 billion, followed by Taiwan with $8.6 billion. Even battered technology funds absorbed $14.5 billion, indicating strong dip-buying behavior amidst the widespread market chaos.
